title: DNS Systems: Name Resolution
subject: DNS
description: Troubleshoot the backbone of the network. Resolve issues with record types, stale data, and external resolution using an evidence-first approach.

tickets.title: "Internal site loads by IP, but not by name"
tickets.summary: Users can reach 'http://172.18.2.50' but get a 'Site Not Found' error when they type 'http://portal.local'.
artifact: Ping portal.local: 'Request could not find host'
DNS Console: No record exists for 'portal'

triage.q: If the IP works but the name doesn't, which system is failing?

diagnosis.q: What is missing in the DNS Forward Lookup Zone?

fix.q: How do you fix the translation?

debrief.summary: DNS is the translator for the network.
debrief.takeaway: Your ping test proved the website was healthy, which narrowed the problem down to a language issue. Adding the 'A' record provided the missing dictionary entry that allows computers to translate the human name into the numerical IP they actually use to talk.

tickets.title: "External websites won't load, but internal ones do"
tickets.summary: Users can access the company intranet, but cannot reach Google or any public websites.

triage.q: If internal sites work but external ones don't, what is the server missing?

diagnosis.q: Why is the server 'blind' to external names?
options: It only knows its own local database and doesn't know where to send unknown queries

fix.q: How do you give the server an 'outside' contact?
options: Add a public DNS (8.8.8.8) to the Forwarders tab

debrief.summary: Forwarders bridge the gap between private and public.
debrief.takeaway: You identified that your server was an expert on your office but had no 'lifeline' to the outside world. By adding a Forwarder, you gave your server a 'phone number' to call whenever it gets a question it can't answer from its own internal list.

tickets.title: "The security log shows 10.0.0.25 is scanning the network"
tickets.summary: You have an IP from a security alert, but you need to find the computer name to identify the owner.

triage.q: Which zone type turns an IP back into a Name?

diagnosis.q: Why did the nslookup command fail?
options: There is no 'PTR' record created for this IP subnet

fix.q: How do you enable 'Caller ID' for these IPs?
options: Create a Reverse Lookup Zone for the 10.0.0.x subnet

debrief.takeaway: You realized that DNS is usually a one-way street (Name to IP). By creating the Reverse Zone, you enabled 'PTR' records. These act like a reverse-phonebook, allowing you to identify 'who' is on your network based on their IP address alone.

tickets.title: "Intermittent errors after moving the web server"
tickets.summary: The web server moved from .20 to .50. Some users see the new site, others see 'Page cannot be displayed'.

triage.q: What happens when a single name has two different 'A' records?
options: DNS uses 'Round Robin' to switch between them

diagnosis.q: Why is the old IP still showing up?

options: Delete the old record and enable Scavenging

debrief.takeaway: You found the 'ghost' record. Because the old address wasn't removed, DNS was essentially flipping a coin—sending some users to the right place and others to a dead end. Cleaning up 'stale' records ensures the phonebook only has one correct answer.

tickets.title: "Marketing wants 'shop.local' to load the web server"
tickets.summary: The team wants users to type 'shop.local' instead of 'web-srv-cluster-01.local'.
artifact: Requirement: Keep the original name for management.

triage.q: Which record type creates an 'Alias' for an existing A-record?

diagnosis.q: Why is a CNAME better than a second A-record?
options: If the server's IP changes, you only update the A-record once

debrief.summary: Aliases separate technical names from user names.
debrief.takeaway: You gave the server a nickname. This makes the network flexible; if you ever replace the server hardware, the marketing link won't break—you just point the nickname to the new machine in the background.

tickets.title: "We can't receive any emails from external clients"
tickets.summary: Employees can send email out, but no external mail is reaching the company's inbox.
artifact: Test: Sending from Gmail results in 'Domain not found'
DNS Console: MX Record is missing

triage.q: Which record tells the world where to deliver your domain's mail?

options: The internet knows your server's name but not its role
Add an MX record pointing to mail.newvue.com

debrief.summary: MX records are the 'Post Office' sign for your domain.
debrief.takeaway: You identified that the 'Mailing Address' was missing. An A-record tells people where a building is, but an MX record tells them it's a Post Office. Without it, the internet didn't know which server was supposed to catch the mail.

tickets.title: "Laptops are taking 5+ minutes to log in at the office"
tickets.summary: Workstations can ping the Domain Controller, but the login screen hangs indefinitely.
artifact: Health Check: The '_msdcs' folder is empty
Error: 'No domain controller could be contacted' (delayed)

triage.q: What record type does Windows use to 'find' AD services?

options: The 'GPS' records for the Login service are missing

fix.q: How do you re-register these records?
options: Restart 'Netlogon' service on the Domain Controller

debrief.summary: SRV records are the 'GPS' for Windows services.
debrief.takeaway: You realized that 'knowing the server exists' isn't enough; the laptops needed to know which server was the 'Login Expert.' Restarting Netlogon causes the DC to re-announce its location and fill in those missing coordinates in DNS.

tickets.title: "The backup DNS server is missing all the new records"
tickets.summary: Records added to DC-01 are not appearing on DC-02, even after 24 hours.
artifact: Zone Properties: 'Allow Zone Transfers' is unchecked

triage.q: What is the process called when a secondary server syncs from a primary?

options: The primary server is 'locking' the data for security

fix.q: How do you unlock the sync?
options: Check 'Allow Zone Transfers' for DC-02's IP

debrief.takeaway: You identified a security gate. DNS servers don't just hand out their entire database to anyone. By enabling the transfer, you 'whitelisted' DC-02, allowing it to pull a fresh copy of the phonebook to stay in sync.

tickets.title: "I'm still pinging the old IP after you said it's fixed"
tickets.summary: You updated 'Server-A' to .100, but the tech at their desk still sees .55.

triage.q: Where does a PC store 'old' DNS answers locally?

diagnosis.q: Why is the tech seeing the wrong IP?
options: Their PC is 'remembering' the old answer

fix.q: How do you force the PC to ask again?

debrief.summary: Local cache can hide server-side updates.
debrief.takeaway: You learned that the 'server' isn't the only one with a memory. The technician's PC was trying to be fast by using an old answer it already had. Flushing the DNS cleared its mind, forcing it to look at the real, updated phonebook.

tickets.title: "External resolution died when our ISP's DNS failed"
tickets.summary: The ISP DNS is down, and now no one can browse the web.
artifact: Setting: 'Use root hints if no forwarders are available' is unchecked

triage.q: What is the 'last resort' method a DNS server uses to find a website?

options: The server isn't allowed to use its backup 'Root Hints'

fix.q: How do you enable the fail-safe?
options: Enable 'Use root hints if no forwarders are available'

debrief.summary: Root Hints are the safety net of the internet.
debrief.takeaway: You found the fail-safe. Using forwarders is like calling a friend for an answer, but Root Hints are like looking it up in the library yourself. Enabling this ensured that even if your ISP fails, your server can still find its own way around the web.
